name: The Knudson Two-Hit Hypothesis
statement: Cancer driven by a tumor-suppressor gene requires two hits that inactivate both of its alleles, one hit often inherited in familial cases.
statementAccent: two hits that inactivate both of its alleles
meaning: The hypothesis holds that both copies of a tumor-suppressor gene must be inactivated, by mutation or epigenetic silencing, before its protective function is lost. In inherited cancer syndromes one defective allele is present from birth, so a single additional somatic hit suffices. In sporadic cases both hits must occur independently in the same cell.
mechanism: A single functional allele of a tumor suppressor is usually enough to restrain uncontrolled growth, so loss of one copy is typically silent. Only when a second event knocks out the remaining allele does the cell lose that brake and progress toward malignancy. Inheriting one hit dramatically raises risk and explains earlier, more frequent, often bilateral tumors.

examples.text: Knudson derived the model from statistics of retinoblastoma: hereditary cases appeared earlier and often in both eyes, consistent with one inherited plus one somatic hit to the RB1 gene.
The model explains why inherited-predisposition cancers strike younger and more multiply than sporadic cancers requiring two independent mutations.
Loss of both alleles underlies syndromes involving genes such as TP53 and BRCA, framed within the two-hit paradigm.

whyItMatters: The hypothesis established the concept of tumor-suppressor genes and recessive cancer predisposition, reshaping cancer genetics. It earned Knudson the 1998 Lasker Clinical Medical Research Award and guides how inherited cancer risk is understood.
limits: Some tumor suppressors show haploinsufficiency, where losing one allele already promotes cancer, so a strict two-hit requirement does not always hold. The model addresses tumor-suppressor loss, not activation of oncogenes, and does not capture the full multistep, multigene nature of tumor development.
misreadings: It does not say every cancer needs exactly two mutations; it specifically concerns biallelic inactivation of tumor-suppressor genes, and inherited cases still require a second somatic hit.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Two-hit hypothesis" article, describing biallelic inactivation of tumor-suppressor genes and the retinoblastoma derivation — supports the statement and examples.
Wikipedia's "Alfred G. Knudson" article, confirming his dates and 1971 formulation of the hypothesis from retinoblastoma statistics — supports the attribution.
